# The Association between Primary Care Appointment Lengths and Opioid Prescribing for Common Pain Conditions

John C. Matulis

Mayo Clinic Kristi Swanson Mayo Clinic Robert D. and Patricia E Rozalina McCoy University of Maryland School of Medicine Research Article Keywords: Schedules and Appointments, Primary Care, Practice Patterns, Opioids, Quality, Safety of Healthcare, Internal Medicine, Family Medicine Posted Date: February 21st, 2024 DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3959740/v1 License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. ## Abstract

Background: While brief duration primary care appointments may improve access, they also limit the time clinicians spend evaluating painful conditions. This study aimed to evaluate whether 15-minute primary care appointments resulted in higher rates of opioid prescribing when compared to ≥ 30-minute appointments. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study using electronic health record (EHR), pharmacy, and administrative scheduling data from five primary care practices in Minnesota. Adult patients seen for acute Evaluation & Management visits between 10/1/2015 and 9/30/2017 scheduled for 15-minute appointments were propensity score matched to those scheduled for ≥ 30-minutes. Sub-groups were analyzed to include patients with acute and chronic pain conditions and prior opioid exposure. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to examine the effects of appointment length on the likelihood of an opioid being prescribed, adjusting for covariates including ethnicity, race, sex, marital status, and prior ED visits and hospitalizations. Results: We identified 45,471 eligible acute primary care visits during the study period with 2.7% (N=1233) of the visits scheduled for 15 minutes and 98.2% (N=44238) scheduled for 30 minutes or longer. Rates of opioid prescribing were significantly lower for opioid naive patients with acute pain scheduled in 15minute appointments when compared to appointments of 30 minutes of longer (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.35-0.84). There were no significant differences in opioid prescribing among other sub-groups. Conclusions: For selected indications and for selected patients, shorter duration appointments may not result in greater rates of opioid prescribing for common painful conditions.

## Background

Of the 50,000 opioid-related overdose deaths reported in 20171, 40% (approximately 20,000 deaths) involved prescribed opioids2. By 2022, annual opioid-related overdoses have increased to over 100,000 deaths per year3. In addition to this staggering death toll, approximately 11.5 million people misuse prescription opioids annually, leading to substantial social and medical harms as well as risk of future addiction and overdose.4 As approximately half of all opioid prescriptions are issued in primary care settings5, responsible opioid stewardship in this setting is critical to managing this public health crisis. Despite efforts to promote standardized practices around oapioid prescribing 6 and the release of national guidelines7 on appropriate prescribing, there is substantial variation in opioid prescribing practices in primary care8–12. Several clinician level factors have been proposed to explain this variation. Training in pain management and substance use disorders among primary care clinicians is variable13 and generally considered inadequate14. Other clinician specific factors include perceived medical contraindications to non-opioid alternatives, the inability of clinicians to address difficult social circumstances which may limit non-opioid treatment options, and a lack of time to perform shared decision-making conversations around opioid prescribing15. However, less is known about how specific organizational factors may impact primary care provider opioid prescribing. While prior study found that primary care appointments scheduled later in the day were associated with increased rates of opioid prescribing16,17, less is known about how other factors like care team support, clinical reosurces and practice structure may impact opioid prescribing. We hypothesize that another organizational factor that may influence opioid prescribing in the primary care setting is the scheduled duration of an acute appointment. While brief duration appointment lengths may help address gaps in access to primary care by increasing the total number of available appointments, they may have unintended consequences on care delivery. When there is inadequate time available to support nuanced and patient centered conversations around different pain management modalities and the risks and benefits of opioid prescribing, clinicians may default to initiating or continuing opioid therapy, potentially deferring difficult conversations, checking the state prescription drug monitoring program, or completing an opioid risk screening tool18. A more detailed understanding of how time pressures may impact opioid prescribing during acute primary care visits may help inform and guide interventions to improve opioid stewardship in the primary care setting.

## Methods

We performed a retrospective cohort study using a combination of institutional billing, scheduling, and pharmacy data from Mayo Clinic, Rochester, MN to compare rates of opioid prescribing as a function of appointment lengths during evaluation and management (E&M) visits for painful conditions rendered within the Mayo Clinic Department of Employee and Community Health (ECH) from 10/1/2015 to 9/30/2017. This study was approved by the Mayo Clinic Internal Review Board (19-001641) and is reported in adherence to STROBE reporting guidelines19.

Mayo Clinic is an integrated healthcare delivery system serving local, regional, national, and international patients with a clinical and academic hub in Rochester, MN. Mayo Clinic’s outpatient department of Employee and Community Health (ECH) provides longitudinal primary care to approximately 120,000 local area residents as well as Mayo Clinic employees and their dependents across five locations in Olmsted County, Minnesota, representing urban, suburban, and rural care settings. The practice employs approximately 55 faculty Internal Medicine physicians, 12 Internal Medicine Nurse Practitioners or Physician’s Assistants, 60 Family Medicine physicians, 35 Family Medicine Nurse Practitioners or Physician’s Assistants, 100 Internal Medicine residents and 25 Family Medicine residents.

We identified adult patients (aged ≥ 18 years) presenting for acute outpatient office (“index”) visits in the Community Internal Medicine (CIM) and Family Medicine (FM) practices of Mayo Clinic, Rochester between 10/1/2015 and 9/30/2017. Included patients were empaneled to a Mayo Clinic primary care provider for at least one year prior to the index visit (to allow for ascertainment of baseline characteristics and risk factors) and for 30 days after (to allow for complete outcome ascertainment). Index visits were identified using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes for office or other outpatient Evaluation & Management (E&M) visits (99201–99215 and 99241–99245). To identify visits for a new chief complaint, we excluded visits preceded by another similarly defined E&M visit in primary care within the preceding two weeks. Visits only for preventive services and visits with non-primary care providers (e.g., Registered Nurse, Licensed Practical Nurse, Certified Nurse Specialist, dietician, social worker, etc.) were excluded from analysis. Patients who did not provide authorization for their data to be used for research were excluded in accordance with Minnesota state law.20

The primary diagnosis from administrative billing data was used to obtain the reason for the visit and was filtered to include common painful conditions routinely managed in primary care, identified through literature review,21–25 authors’ clinical experience, and feedback from subject matter experts. These conditions were identified using ICD-9 and ICD-10 diagnosis codes, as well as the Clinical Classification Software Refined categories developed by the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project26. Both forward mapping (ICD-9 to ICD-10) and backward mapping (ICD-10 to ICD-9) was performed using the General Equivalence Mappings27to enumerate all relevant diagnosis codes of interest for the study period examined. The ICD-10 codes for the full list of selected conditions are presented in Appendix A. Common painful conditions were categorized as acute or chronic by author review (RGM and JCM). In the event of disagreement, a consensus process was used to categorize the diagnosis codes as either acute or chronic. If the authors determined a diagnosis code could plausibly be either acute or chronic, a look back period of 12 months was examined, excluding the 30 days directly prior to the index visit (because that would have disqualified this visit from being included in the dataset). If another visit with a similar indication was identified during this time, the condition was considered chronic, otherwise it was considered acute.

The main exposure of interest was the scheduled appointment length of the index visit. Appointment lengths were ascertained from administrative scheduling data and categorized as 15 minutes (brief duration) versus 30 minutes or longer (long duration). The length of time allotted for a particular appointment is usually determined by centralized scheduling staff members using standardized scheduling templates (Appendix B) based on the patient’s stated health concern and patient characteristics; however, schedulers and primary care physicians may substitute their own judgement and schedule patients into longer or briefer appointment slots as deemed appropriate to meet patient needs.

Covariates of interest included patient and clinician level factors. Patient characteristics extracted from the EHR included age, ethnicity, race, sex, marital status, and geographic location. Limited English proficiency was identified from registration data. Using ICD-9 and ICD-10 diagnosis codes from billing data, the Deyo adaptation of the Charlson comorbidity index was calculated with severity weighting incorporated28–30. Provider level covariates included primary care specialty (Internal Medicine vs. Family Medicine), Clinician type (NP/PA, physician, or resident).

The primary outcome was whether an opioid medication was prescribed on the same day as the index visit. Data on opioid prescribing was ascertained from electronic order entry within the EHR and linked to the study population based on the ordering date of the prescription.

Opioid use in the 6 months prior to the index visit was obtained from EHR prescription data to determine whether a patient was opioid naïve (no prior opioid prescription issued in the preceding 6 months) or had prior opioid exposure (any prior opioid prescription issued within the past 6 months).

Patient and visit characteristics were summarized for all eligible visits, which were subset into four mutually exclusive categories: acute pain–opioid naïve patient, acute pain–prior opioid use patient, chronic pain–opioid naïve patient, chronic pain– prior opioid use patient. Patient characteristics were summarized in aggregate and compared across differing appointment lengths to assess for significant associations using Chi-Square tests for categorical variables and Kruskal-Wallis tests for continuous variables. The distribution of appointment lengths was summarized across the four subgroups. It was anticipated that the length of scheduled appointments would depend on certain patient and system level factors (i.e., medical complexity, social support, triage criteria, etc.). Therefore, propensity score methods by means of covariate adjustment were used to account for potential selection bias in the exposure of interest. Full details regarding the propensity score matching approach used are provided in Appendix C. Multivariate logistic regression was performed to examine the effects of appointment length on the likelihood of an opioid being prescribed, while adjusting for other covariates, including ethnicity, race, sex, marital status, and prior ED visits and hospitalizations. A separate model was computed and reported for each of the four subgroups. The calculated propensity score for each observation was included as a separate covariate in each of the models. Odds ratio (OR) estimates were computed, along with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI) and p-values, for each model. All data management and analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc. Cary, NC).

## Results

We identified 45,471 eligible acute care visits to primary care during the study period. Both brief and longer duration appointments were evenly distributed between the practice areas (Table 1), with 2.7% (N = 1233) of the visits being brief duration (15 minutes) and 98.2% (N = 44238) scheduled for 30 minutes of longer. There were no significant differences in opioid prescribing among the other three subgroups (Fig. 1). ## Discussion

Brief, 15-min primary care appointments for acute and chronic painful health conditions, as implemented across five primary care clinics within an integrated healthcare delivery system in the U.S. Upper Midwest, did not increase the likelihood of opioid prescribing. Among opioid-naïve patients presenting for evaluation of an acute pain syndrome, brief duration appointment length was associated with significantly lower odds of opioid initiation compared to longer appointments. There was no difference in the odds of opioid prescribing for patients with chronic pain (whether opioid-naïve or not) or for patients already on opioid therapy. These findings underscore the prevailing caution around opioid prescribing and hesitation to initiate therapy for new episodes of pain in patients not already receiving opioid analgesia. These findings lend important insights into the impact of limited time spent with patients and time available for shared decision-making about pain management options and opioid prescribing. Our work builds on emerging literature suggesting that organizational and practice management variables within primary care may contribute to opioid prescribing practices. Neprash et al16 and Philpot et al17 have studied the association between time of the day and opioid prescription patterns, identifying that rates of opioid prescriptions increased later in the clinic day. Other clinician and system factors impacting opioid prescribing have also been identified15, including lack of comfort in discontinuing previously prescribed opioids, lack of control over opioids prescribed by other clinicians outside of primary care, and limited access to comprehensive pain management programs. However, to our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between scheduled appointment length and rates of opioid prescribing. Similarly, while much has been written about the relationship between time pressures on physicians, burnout, and the quality-of-care provided31,32, and some published on the impact of time constraints on resource utilization in primary care practice33, there was little evidence about the relationship between appointment duration and the plausible impact on the quality of clinical care provided, such as opioid prescribing. The scheduling template utilized by our healthcare system prompts the scheduling of brief (15-minute) appointments for a limited number of painful conditions (Appendix B), which explains both the small number of 15-minute appointments and the lower odds of opioid prescribing observed during these encounters. Specifically, patients with underlying medical complexity as well as patients presenting for the evaluation of most musculoskeletal conditions are preferentially scheduled for longer duration appointments. Despite efforts to minimize confounding by patient factors that permit shorter appointment scheduling and select the subset of patients scheduled for 30-minute appointments who would be just as likely to have been scheduled for 15-minute appointments, it is likely that residual unmeasured confounding remained. # Increasing digital equity to promote online smoking cessation program engagement among rural adults: a randomized controlled pilot trial

## Abstract

Background Cigarette smoking prevalence is higher for rural than urban adults, yet digital access to cessation programming is reduced. We aim to investigate digital access interventions to promote engagement with an online evidence-based cessation treatment (EBCT) program among rural adults. Methods This pilot trial used a pragmatic, three-arm, randomized, parallel-group design (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05209451). Inclusion criteria included being aged ≥18, Mayo Clinic Midwest patient, rural residency, and currently smokes cigarettes. All participants received an online, 12-week EBCT program and were randomized to receive one of three digital access interventions: print materials (control, n = 30); print materials + loaner iPad device with data plan coverage (n = 30); or print materials + loaner device + up to six, 15-20-minute motivational interviewing-based coaching calls to support technology needs (n = 30). A composite score of trial engagement (primary outcome) and self-reported smoking abstinence and use of EBCT resources (secondary outcomes) were assessed online at 4 and 12 weeks. Qualitative interviews were used to assess patient experience. Neither participants nor outcome assessors were blinded to group assignment. Results Results are reported for all 30 participants in each group. The average age of participants is 51.0 years and 61% are women. We show no significant arm differences for the trial engagement composite score (p = 0.30). We also find coaching support is significantly (p < 0.05) associated with enhanced smoking-related treatment response, including cigarette abstinence and use of EBCT resources, and participants reported positive experiences with the intervention. Conclusions The coaching intervention to support technology needs is acceptable and shows preliminary evidence of its efficacy in smoking-related treatment response. Further studies could refine and implement the coaching intervention for trial engagement and long-term cessation.

Rural communities in the United States (US) experience marked health disparities, including higher risk of chronic disease, worse health status, and increased mortality compared to their urban counterparts ( https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/people-in-rural-areas-die-athigher-rates-than-those-in-urban-areas/ ) [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . A major contributor to these observed health inequalities is cigarette smoking, which is more prevalent among rural compared to urban adults in the US (26% vs. 21%) 7 . Furthermore, a recent study found that the odds of quitting smoking were significantly lower in rural compared to urban areas 8 . Because cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable death in the US 9 , promoting cessation among rural populations is foundational to eliminating existing health disparities.

## Plain Language Summary

More adults smoke cigarettes in rural than urban adults, yet there is less access to effective digital tools to assist people to quit smoking in rural areas. We compared three strategies to promote engagement with an online program to encourage rural adults to quit smoking. The three interventions were: print materials; print materials plus a loaner iPad device with data plan coverage; or print materials and loaner device, plus up to six, 15-20-minute individualized coaching calls to support technology needs. We found that individuals receiving the coaching support had improved smoking-related outcomes.

Our study provides a better understanding of the resources needed to support digital access in rural populations and the results could be used to improve approaches to encourage people living in rural areas to stop smoking.

Structural barriers that impede rural residents' access to cessation support include local clinician shortages, travel costs required for face-toface visits, and higher rates of uninsurance 7, 10 . Such barriers to in-person services provide an opportunity to promote free, digital, evidence-based smoking cessation treatments (EBCTs). These include text messaging applications, coaching, and pharmacotherapy provided by state quitlines 11 . However, many rural dwellers lack the hardware, connectivity, and familiarity with digital technologies that are required to utilize these treatments. National survey data indicate that compared to urban residents, rural residents are less likely to have access to a digital device (i.e., smartphone, tablet) and broadband (BB) internet ( https://www.pewresearch.org/shortreads/2021/08/19/some-digital-divides-persist-between-rural-urban-andsuburban-america/ ) and report lower levels of digital literacy 12, 13 . Digital inclusivity has been identified as a social determinant of health [14] [15] [16] . National programs highlight the need for translational research into effective, scalable techquity strategies that promote digital access and literacy among underserved populations ( https://www.internetforall.gov/sites/default/files/2022-05/digital-equity-act-info-sheet.pdf ) 17 .

Fortunately, reports suggest that some strategies may help to neutralize the digital divide. These include technical training and assistance programs 18, 19 , digital navigators 20 , tailored technology support 21, 22 , and digital literacy programs 23 . Evidence remains sparse, yet, to date, effect sizes have been modest and varied across populations worldwide. Research has not explored the use of such strategies among rural populations who smoke.

We, therefore, sought to assess if multiple concurrent strategies would be more impactful on engagement with and response to an online program for smoking cessation among US Midwest rural adults with digital access barriers who smoke cigarettes. We did so using a mixed-methods, randomized, controlled pilot trial called the IDEA (Increasing Digital Equity and Access) study 24 . The study compared three digital health access interventions of varying intensity -print materials only (control), print materials + a loaner digital device, and print materials + a loaner digital device + coaching support to address digital literacy -for engagement with an online smoking cessation program. We hypothesized that trial engagement and smoking abstinence would be higher for the intervention that included coaching support compared with the other arms. We used qualitative interviews to assess patient experience with the interventions and feasibility of remote trial participation. We show no significant arm differences for a composite score of trial engagement; but coaching support was associated with enhanced smoking-related treatment response, including cigarette abstinence and use of EBCT resources, and participants reported positive experiences with the intervention.

## Methods

The trial was designed in accordance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement for pilot and feasibility trials 25 , and is registered with the Clinical Trials Registry (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05209451; registration date January 25, 2022). The study protocol 24 was guided by the Digital Health Equity Framework 15 and co-designed with a Midwest rural community advisory committee (CAC) to maximize relevance to rural populations. The first participant was accrued on February 11, 2022, and the last participant on November 18, 2022. Data were collected from January 2022 through March 2023. The trial is completed.

## Ethics

We obtained approval of the study protocol from the Mayo Clinic Institutional Review Board (IRB 21-011617), and the authors complied with all relevant ethical regulations in conducting the study. Written informed consent was obtained from all trial participants.

## Trial design

This pilot trial utilized a pragmatic, three-arm, randomized, parallel-group design. Before the trial, the study statistician generated the random allocation sequence, and participants completed baseline measures before being informed of their assignment. Participants were stratified based on the state of residence (Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa) and randomized with 1:1:1 allocation to one of three study arms. All participants were provided with an online smoking cessation program and randomized to receive one of three digital access interventions: print materials only (control condition), print materials + a loaner iPad device, or print materials + loaner iPad device + tailored coaching support. All randomized participants were asked to complete online study assessments and remotely conducted breath carbon monoxide (CO) testing at 4-and 12-weeks post-randomization. At the study's end, we randomly sampled 10 participants from each study arm to participate in an individual qualitative interview regarding their experience with the interventions. Neither participants nor outcome assessors were blinded to group assignment. We mailed participants a $25 cash card as remuneration for completing the baseline survey and $50 for completing each follow-up assessment (2 surveys and 2 breath CO testings); up to $225 total. Individuals randomly selected for and completing the interview received another $75. The pre-specified primary outcome was a composite measure of trial engagement, and secondary outcomes were self-reported smoking abstinence, use of EBCT, and patient experience.

## Participant recruitment and screening

From January 2022 through November 2022, research staff recruited adult patients from Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, and the Mayo Clinic Health System (MCHS). The MCHS is a regional network of community clinics, hospitals, and other healthcare facilities with a physical presence in 44 communities in southeast Minnesota, western Wisconsin, and northeastern Iowa ( https://www.mayoclinichealthsystem.org/about-us ).

We used the Mayo Clinic electronic health record (EHR) to recruit study participants. We identified patients with (1) authorization for the use of their medical record for research; (2) a Mayo Clinic visit at a Rochester/ MCHS site during a preceding two-year period; (3) aged 18 or older; (4) current smoking/tobacco use status as reported in the EHR; (5) address in Minnesota, Wisconsin, or Iowa; and (6) Rural resident based on Rural-Urban Commuting Area (RUCA) codes 4-10 ( https://www.hrsa.gov/ruralhealth/about-us/what-is-rural ) derived from the ZIP code of current or last known address. About 61,929 current smokers were within this sampling frame. We mailed invitation letters to random samples of 525 patients each (with equal numbers in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Iowa) until we achieved our targeted sample size of 90 participants. Non-respondents were contacted three weeks after the initial mailing by phone and email; up to three total contacts were made.

The invitation letter contained (1) the study-specific email address and toll-free number that participants could contact for more information and screening and (2) a URL link to a screening questionnaire. To enhance credibility, the invitation included a URL link to the study on the Mayo Clinic Clinical Trials webpage and a Mayo Clinic business card with the study contact information. Patients could decline participation and further contact by phone, email, or postal mail.

## Study eligibility criteria

The study inclusion criteria were: (1) A Mayo Clinic Midwest patient (Mayo Clinic Rochester or Mayo Clinic Health System [MCHS]) with a Mayo Clinic number; (2) Aged 18 years or older; (3) Can read and speak in the English language. Based on 2019 data, 97% of our Rochester and MCHS patients speak English. The study will provide all participants with a smoking cessation program delivered through the Mayo Clinic patient portal. Currently, Mayo Clinic's portal services are not offered in languages other than English; (4) Has a Minnesota, Wisconsin, or Iowa address currently or at date of most recent visit to Mayo Clinic Rochester or MCHS; (5) Rural resident based on RUCA codes derived from ZIP code of current or last known address; (6) Has access to a telephone of any type (e.g., landline, smartphone). Access to a telephone is needed to complete the coaching support intervention and to follow-up with participants if there are issues with accessing the patient portal for the smoking cessation intervention; (7) Current smoker defined as one or more cigarettes (even a puff) smoked in the past 30 days (original criteria). This definition allows for enrollment of non-daily and/or light smoking enhancing the generalizability. In addition to cigarettes, cigarillos and cigars are combustible tobacco products and thus relevant as a focus for our study. Thus, the protocol was modified with IRB approval to change this criterion to include other combustible tobacco use. The final criterion was "Current smoker defined as one or more cigarettes, cigarillos, or cigars (even a puff) smoked in the past 30 days." To enhance the generalizability of our findings, we will enroll participants using other tobacco/nicotine products if cigarette, cigarillo or cigar smoking is the primary product used; (8) For past 3 months not enrolled in a program or use of cessation pharmacotherapy. The protocol was modified with IRB approval to allow for ad hoc use to enhance generalizability. The final criterion was "For past 3 months not enrolled in a program or use of cessation pharmacotherapy other than ad hoc use, for example, used nicotine gum or lozenge once or twice"; (9) Willing to make a quit smoking attempt; (10) Has a patient portal account, or is willing to create a patient portal account; (11) Has an email address to provide to study staff, or is willing to create an email address; and (12) Has digital access barriers defined by one of more of the following: (a) based on participant ZIP code from current or last known address geocoded census block group indicates an area of poor BB coverage ( https://www.fcc.gov/ ); (b) no existing Mayo Clinic patient portal account or (c) has a Mayo Clinic patient portal account but has not used it in the past 5 years; (c) self-reports having no access to broadband (high speed) internet connection for personal use; and/or (e) self-reports low digital literacy defined with the screening question "How comfortable are you using technology to manage your health care remotely? For example, using patient online services (i.e., patient portal) to schedule appointments, check for test results, or send a message to your provider" (included: not at all or a little comfortable).

Exclusion criteria were: (1) Anyone not meeting all inclusion criteria will be excluded; and (2) Has participated in a behavioral smoking cessation program in the past 3 months.

## Informed consent process and baseline survey

Interested screen-eligible individuals provided informed consent using a paper form or electronically via DocuSign. Individuals completed a baseline survey using a paper form that was returned using a postage-paid return envelope or electronically by responding to a URL link. Research staff enrolled and randomized individuals who provided informed consent and completed the baseline survey.

## Enrollment materials and smoking cessation program

We mailed all randomized participants a welcome letter and written information on how to set up a patient online services account, access to free telephone support (Patient Portal Helpline), and links for portal technical support, including an online instructional video for accessing and using the patient portal. All participants were mailed an iCOquit® Smokelyzer and instructions on its use for breath carbon monoxide (CO) tests to biochemically verify smoking status at follow-up assessments (see Measures). We also mailed participants intervention materials based on their study arm assignment.

Participants in all three study arms received a 12-week, online, smoking cessation program through Mayo Clinic's patient portal. The program commenced within 1 week after randomization, but if the participant needed to set up a portal account, it began 1 week after their account registration. The program linked participants to free, evidence-based, digital, tailored, interactive, Smokefree.gov web resources ( https://smokefree.gov/ ). Research supporting this approach indicates that 3-5% of individuals who quit without treatment maintain abstinence, but when cessation resources include behavioral counseling and pharmacotherapy, the chance of success is up to threefold higher 26 . Smokefree.gov resources include a website tailored to readiness to quit smoking, a quit plan, a toll-free number (1-800-QUIT-NOW) and weblink to state quitlines that offer free cessation coaching and pharmacotherapy, texting program, smartphone applications, online live chat, and social media platforms 11 . These resources offer complementary technology options to meet individual needs and preferences. Among a national sample of adults (N = 1308), providing Smokefree.gov web resources resulted in a 12-month smoking abstinence rate of 26%, comparable to the efficacy of other behavioral interventions for smoking cessation 27 .

The smoking cessation program was entirely asynchronous. Study staff sent participants one weekly message for 12 weeks. The messages provided simplified navigation to specific EBCT resources in Smokefree.gov and the opportunity to answer 1-4 self-reflective questions about their cessation journey relevant to that week's message (see Supplementary Method 1). properties.title: Increasing digital equity to promote online smoking cessation program engagement among rural adults: a randomized controlled pilot trial
properties.abstract: Cigarette smoking prevalence is higher for rural than urban adults, yet digital access to cessation programming is reduced. We aim to investigate digital access interventions to promote engagement with an online evidence-based cessation treatment (EBCT) program among rural adults. This pilot trial used a pragmatic, three-arm, randomized, parallel-group design (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05209451). Inclusion criteria included being aged ≥18, Mayo Clinic Midwest patient, rural residency, and currently smokes cigarettes. All participants received an online, 12-week EBCT program and were randomized to receive one of three digital access interventions: print materials (control, n = 30); print materials + loaner iPad device with data plan coverage (n = 30); or print materials + loaner device + up to six, 15–20-minute motivational interviewing-based coaching calls to support technology needs (n = 30). A composite score of trial engagement (primary outcome) and self-reported smoking abstinence and use of EBCT resources (secondary outcomes) were assessed online at 4 and 12 weeks. Qualitative interviews were used to assess patient experience. Neither participants nor outcome assessors were blinded to group assignment. Results are reported for all 30 participants in each group. The average age of participants is 51.0 years and 61% are women. We show no significant arm differences for the trial engagement composite score (p = 0.30). We also find coaching support is significantly (p < 0.05) associated with enhanced smoking-related treatment response, including cigarette abstinence and use of EBCT resources, and participants reported positive experiences with the intervention. The coaching intervention to support technology needs is acceptable and shows preliminary evidence of its efficacy in smoking-related treatment response. Further studies could refine and implement the coaching intervention for trial engagement and long-term cessation. More adults smoke cigarettes in rural than urban adults, yet there is less access to effective digital tools to assist people to quit smoking in rural areas. We compared three strategies to promote engagement with an online program to encourage rural adults to quit smoking. The three interventions were: print materials; print materials plus a loaner iPad device with data plan coverage; or print materials and loaner device, plus up to six, 15–20-minute individualized coaching calls to support technology needs. We found that individuals receiving the coaching support had improved smoking-related outcomes. Our study provides a better understanding of the resources needed to support digital access in rural populations and the results could be used to improve approaches to encourage people living in rural areas to stop smoking. Kelpin et al. present results from a randomized controlled pilot trial comparing 3 digital access and literacy intervention strategies for enhancing access to online evidence-based smoking cessation treatment among Midwest rural adults who smoke. Findings suggest individual phone coaching to address technology needs may improve smoking outcomes.

# Social Capital: A Remedy for Deaths of Despair in the Rust Belt US Counties?

Asst. Prof. Dr. Murat Bayraktar

Istanbul Esenyurt University https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4028-192X

Research Article Keywords: Social capital, loneliness, deaths of despair, rust belt, public policy. Posted Date: June 6th, 2024 DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-4532220/v1 License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Read Full License Additional Declarations: The authors declare no competing interests.

## Abstract

This study emphasizes how crucial social capital to decrease the deaths of despair among Rust Belt counties. From the year 2015 the social theory of “deaths of despair” became a matter of curiosity among researchers: rising despair and unemployment in regions like the Rust Belt were the common cause of rising death rates among white Americans. Suicide, alcoholic liver disease, and drug overdose are the three categories of disease. The Appalachian region of the United States, particularly Pennsylvania, West Virginia, along with Delaware, has a high rate of diseases of despair and the deaths that follow. Numerous things, such as hopelessness, loneliness, loss, or a lack of direction or purpose in life, can contribute to despair. When researchers test the validity of this hypothesis, mixed results have been found in this regard. Findings from 140 counties from the Rust Belt region revealed that social capital can be an effective policy instrument to decrease the deaths of despair. Therefore federal, state, county, academia and community leaders should implement policies to increase the social capital levels among US citizens. JEL Codes: H10, H75, I15, I18

## 1. Introduction

There is a deadly drug epidemic in the United States right now. Between 1999 and 2016, the number of drug-related deaths in the United States increased from 16,849 to 63,632 (Hedegaard et al., 2017). Downward intergenerational mobility, income stagnation, and broken social and family relations are the main components of what Case and Deaton refer to as cumulative disadvantage, according to their preliminary explanatory framework (King et al., 2022). The economists Case and Deaton revealed in 2015 that middle-aged non-Hispanic White people with low levels of education were experiencing an increase in premature mortality, and that decades-long achieves in US life expectancy had stopped and even reversed. They proposed that the rise in cause specific mortality from drug overdoses, alcohol liver disease, and suicides was the cause of this premature mortality. They further proposed that hopelessness brought on by unfavorable social and economic conditions was the root cause of these increases in cause-specific mortality. It gave rise to the widely accepted narrative of people dying of despair (Shanahan and Copeland, 2021). Suicide, drug poisoning, and alcohol-related deaths have all increased, contributing to the US's declining life expectancy. To guide public health initiatives, it is necessary to determine whether or not patterns associated with these causes differ (Shiels et al., 2020). A systematic review (Vowles et al., 2015) discovered that in the US, between 21 and 29 percent of patients who are prescribed opioids over chronic pain abuse them. Evidence that prescription opioid abuse is causally linked to a higher risk of heroin use in adolescence was also discovered by a novel longitudinal study (Kelley-Quon et al., 2019).

In the United States, drug poisonings, alcohol-related causes, and suicide have all seen sharp increases in death rates, with middle-aged White, American Indian, and Alaska Native men as well as women experiencing the greatest increases (Shiels et al., 2017; Case & Deaton, 2015; 2017; Stein et al., 2017; Woolf et al., 2018). Between 2015 to 2017, there were yearly decreases in the US life expectancy due to increases in midlife mortality (Kochanek et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2015). It has been proposed that rising rates of unemployment and financial instability are societal factors at the core of these increases (Case & Deaton, 2017). Among Black and Latino people, premature mortality decreased from 2000–03 to 2012–15, while among White people, it increased in many US counties. Nationwide, the death rate from drug poisoning rose in every county. Between 2000 and 2015, white individuals aged 25 to 64 showed significant increases in both urban and rural counties, regardless of their socioeconomic status (Shiels et al., 2019). There have been documented notable increases in alcohol-related deaths in the US during the previous 20 years. Comprehensive evaluations of the patterns in alcohol-related mortality by age, sex, race/ethnicity, along with social and geographic variables are, however, absent (Spillane et al., 2020). Landberg (2008) discovered that in Eastern European spirit-consuming nations (Poland, Belarus, and Russia), an increase in the average person's alcohol intake of 1 liter was linked to a 5.7–7.5% rise in overall suicide rates. Accidents and liver disorders are also closely associated with excessive alcohol consumption, particularly risky binge drinking. Additionally, there is a direct correlation between stress and hopelessness and suicide and cardiovascular illnesses (Razvodovsky, 2013; Brainerd, 2001). After state socialism collapsed, drug abuse also skyrocketed in Eastern Europe, although its overall impact on the mortality rate crisis is negligible (King et al., 2022). According to King et al. (2009), they also discovered that privatization was linked to deaths, mostly of working-age men, and that it also predicted alcohol use, suicide, being unemployed, and acute heart disease. The loss of nearly two years of life expectancy for men and 0.7 years for women was linked, according to the authors, to extreme privatization policies. Furthermore, (King et al., 2022) radical privatization was equivalent to depriving these workers of their de facto property rights, which Soviet-style companies granted to their workers. This greatly increased stress and uncertainty. Along with many other social benefits, these companies gave their workers a sense of purpose and belonging. All of these were compromised by privatization. The author, Rozalina McCoy, M.D., a primary care physician and endocrinologist, pointed out that in 2020, COVID-19 was either the cause or a contributing factor in nearly 10% of all deaths in Minnesota. One of the main causes of these deaths, particularly for older adults living in rural areas, was social isolation (Jacobbi, 2023) Although loneliness is not new, there seems to be a growing awareness of it in terms of social and health issues. In 2018 and 2021, the UK and Japan, respectively, appointed ministers of loneliness (Lancet, 2023). Standardized and approved measuring instruments should be used to include loneliness in general health surveillance that covers a wider range of age and geographic areas (Surkalim et al., 2022). While not exclusive to the US, these health catastrophes are uncommon. An unparalleled mortality crisis struck Eastern Europe thirty years ago as former socialist nations made the shift to capitalism, foreshadowing the epidemic of deaths from despair that is plaguing the region today (Eberstadt, 2010). The relationship between social capital, health, and well-being has garnered attention recently, and the idea of social capital has grown in significance in public health research and health promotion (Putnam, 2000; Islam et al., 2006).

## 2. Deaths of Despair (DoD)

In the 21st century, self-harm and substance use disorders are becoming increasingly common causes of death by despair for people at the bottom of the social hierarchy. This is a hallmark of American society. Depressing deaths are largely caused by socioeconomic disruptions, which also influence other primary causes of health disparities and healthcare behavior (King et al., 2022). The United States was already dealing alongside a crisis of hopelessness and deaths from alcohol poisoning, overdoses, and suicides when the COVID pandemic struck, shocking society in a way never seen before. Two conclusions are highlighted by our results: Because results from different datasets can differ significantly, researchers looking into trends in behavioral and mental wellness should exercise caution when relying excessively on one. Ans, years later, there may be a correlation between higher rates of overdose and suicide in metropolitan areas with high rates of anxiety and depression (Dobson et al., 2022). By 2015, US life expectancy stopped, may be caused by the high death rate among manual laborers from drug and alcohol abuse as well as suicide. The phrase "deaths of despair" was first used by economists Angus Deaton and Anne Case to describe a growing health crisis among the poorest segments of the American population. They calculate that from the turn of the century, over half a million unnecessary deaths have resulted from such despair, which is rooted in strong social convulsions caused by rapid declines in industry (Case & Deaton 2020). In the US, up until 2018–19, patterns in deaths from despair were stable and showed that White people with less education had higher rates of despair and mortality, while low-income minorities had lower rates of these deaths and high levels of optimism (Graham & Pinto 2019). The United States is seeing an increase in midlife non-Hispanic white mortality, especially in small metro along with rural counties (Parsons & Barger, 2019). Between 2001 and 2016, there was a significant increase in DoD mortality within England and Wales, with male rates consistently higher than female rates. The increase in drug-related fatalities is the main cause of the rise. Suicide, alcohol-related deaths, and drug poisoning all showed increases during this time period, but at the national level, their trends did not tightly coincide (Augarde et al., 2022). Mortality rates in Scotland are higher than in other nations of Western Europe, even after deprivation is taken into consideration. This "excess" mortality is a result of higher rates of violence, suicide, and drug and alcohol-related deaths (DRDs), especially in young adults. The recent increases in alcohol-related deaths along with suicide can be explained by age-period and cohort effects, respectively (Parkinson et al., 2018). The public health research has addressed the issue of ignoring the burden of mortality related to mental health issues extensively. To enhance policy and gain a deeper understanding of national and international mental health issues, pertinent scientific data from the societies with the highest rates of mental health death are crucial. Three Baltic States—Estonia, Lithuania, and Latvia—are nations in Central and Eastern Europe that have had severe trauma following the Soviet transition and have some of the highest rates of alcohol-related and suicide-related deaths in the continent. When estimating the overall burden of mortality related to mental health issues, the Baltic States along with other post-soviet nations should take into account the proportions of different external factors of death as well as alcohol related reasons of death (Stumbrys et al., 2022). Apart from the COVID-19 patients' illnesses, social distancing measures, mandatory lockdowns, and a variety of psychosocial factors have caused mental health issues for isolated individuals and the general public. During the pandemic, the incidence of anxiety and depression has increased significantly (Zhu et al., 2023). According to Zhou et al., during the COVID-19 outbreak, the prevalence of anxiety and depression symptoms within Chinese high school students was 37.4% and 43.7%, respectively (Zhu et al., 2020). Older adults (over 50) were identified as another group susceptible for mental health issues in a different study (Tian et al., 2020) presumably as a result of ageism, inactivity, and loneliness (Creese et al., 2021; Bergman et al., 2020). In India's northeastern state and eastern state of West Bengal, the study examines the relationship between the substance use within scheduled tribe men—who are primarily recognized for their primitivism, isolation, insecurity, and social, educational, as well as economic regression—and non scheduled tribe men. Middle-aged men who work in unorganized jobs, practice different religions, come from lower socioeconomic quintiles, have been divorced, separated, abandoned, or widowed have significantly higher rates of substance use, according to a study that correlated substance use with socioeconomic characteristics (Barman & Chowdhury, 2023). Suicide is the third most common cause of death in the United States and the fourth most common cause of death for young people globally (Hughes et al., 2023). The year 2020 saw suicide account for almost 20 percent of all youth fatalities in the US (CDC, 2023). Although the full impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on youth suicide is still unknown, preliminary data indicate that the US suicide rate is generally rising, with young people from minority groups suffering a disproportionate share of the increase (Curtin et al., 2022). Before the pandemic, young people and children in the UK had declining mental health, and the social, educational, and health outcomes for kids with mental health disorders are worse than they were for earlier generations (Sellers et al., 2019). Anxiety, depression, as well as self-harm increased between 2004 and 2017, especially in adolescent girls (Sadler et al., 2017). Whether or not there is a pandemic, people who are most at risk of experiencing poor mental health outcomes need to have access to preventive mental health interventions (Hjorthøj & Madsen, 2023). There is still much to learn about the factors preventing youth suicide. Strong interpersonal relationships, faith/spiritual factors, family cohesion, improved access to care, cognitive flexibility, and emotion regulation abilities have all been linked to preventing suicidal behavior within young people (Abraham & Sher, 2017; Droege et al., 2017; Robinson et al., 2022; Dorol-Beauroy-Eustache & Mishara, 2021; Allen et al., 2022). While some negative aspects of social media and the internet have raised concerns, some positive aspects, like community, connection, and decreased isolation, may actually be protective (Marchant et al., 2017). The evaluation of social connectedness to be a potential target for clinical risk assessment and suicide prevention tactics is becoming more prevalent (King et al., 2019). The correlation between suicidality and intersecting marginalized identities was considerably lowered by family support, highlighting a possible area for intervention (Hughes et al., 2023). The epidemic of depressive deaths can be linked to modern globalization in many cases. Remarkably, marginalized as well as indebted farmers in India have one of the highest rates of suicide globally as a result of the agricultural sector's liberalization in the 1990s (Kennedy & King, 2014). According to a report by the US National Academy of Sciences, mortality is declining in 16 developed countries (Western Europe, Canada, Australia, as well as Japan). It has been noted that humans are limited by evolutionary strategy in requiring social support throughout their entire life cycle. When there is no support, problems mount and it appears that there is no way out. The sixteen wealthy nations offer collective support at every level, thereby enabling multiple routes forward and shielding people and families from hopelessness. By using the 16-nation control group's best practices, the US could resolve its health crisis (Sterling & Platt, 2022). The United States has experienced a rise in mortality rates, which can be attributed in part to an increase in alcohol and drug poisoning, suicide, and heart disease as a result of increasing obesity.Deaths from despair are mostly caused by isolation on the rise and attempts by individuals to self-medicate in order to make up for dopamine deficiency in the brain (Freeborn, 2022).

## 3. Loneliness

Perlman and Peplau (1982) define loneliness as an individual's desired as well as achieved degrees of social relations not matching, which leads to a subjective, unpleasant, along with distressing phenomenon. Therefore, it is possible to argue that loneliness results from a sense of a mismatch between one's desired degree and/or quality of relationships and those that actually exist. Loneliness, or the lack of it, is frequently used to indicate mental well-being in correlation with mental health measures, particularly in older adults (Luanaigh & Lawlor, 2008). The majority of studies concentrate on the elderly, so (Mansfield et al., 2019) suggest doing research that looks at a larger range of age groups in various social contexts and/or that takes a defined life course perspective. According to some philosophers, loneliness is a common human experience (Rotenberg, 1999; Mijuskovic, 1981). In their definition of connectedness, it means a feeling that arises from safe and enduring relationships throughout families, schools, and communities—a sense of being looked after, supported, belonging, and close to others (DiClemente et al., 2009). Similarly, the Harvard Study of Adult Development found that individuals with strong ties to their family, community, and school outlive, are healthier, happier, and live longer than their less connected peers, based on a 70-year follow-up of over 700 men. A happier, healthier life is facilitated by relationships in all of their forms, including those found in book clubs, Bible study groups, families, coworkers, romantic partnerships, and tennis partners (Waldinger & Schulz, 2023). The data revealed three different but related conceptualizations of loneliness: existential, emotional, and social. The results will be helpful in public policy as well as practice decision-making that aims to determine who experiences loneliness, why it happens, how to deal with it, and the best strategies for minimizing loneliness or maximizing its benefits for better wellness and health outcomes. In our review, social loneliness was the main topic of most studies (Mansfield et al., 2021). Table 1 Parts of loneliness Loneliness • emotional loneliness • social loneliness • existential loneliness Source: Mansfield et al., 2019

Loneliness is a topic that has gained attention due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which has forced many people to rearrange their work schedules and require physical distance during certain times. There's no denying the health risks. An increased risk of infectious diseases, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, depression, and anxiety is linked to a lack of social connections. A meta-analysis of data coming from 113 nations (Surkalim et al., 2022) demonstrates that loneliness has become a global problem, with a significant fraction of the population experiencing problematic degrees of loneliness in many of these nations. properties.abstract: Abstract This study emphasizes how crucial social capital to decrease the deaths of despair among Rust Belt counties. From the year 2015 the social theory of “deaths of despair” became a matter of curiosity among researchers: rising despair and unemployment in regions like the Rust Belt were the common cause of rising death rates among white Americans. Suicide, alcoholic liver disease, and drug overdose are the three categories of disease. The Appalachian region of the United States, particularly Pennsylvania, West Virginia, along with Delaware, has a high rate of diseases of despair and the deaths that follow. Numerous things, such as hopelessness, loneliness, loss, or a lack of direction or purpose in life, can contribute to despair. When researchers test the validity of this hypothesis, mixed results have been found in this regard. Findings from 140 counties from the Rust Belt region revealed that social capital can be an effective policy instrument to decrease the deaths of despair. ### Introduction

The Inflation Reduction Act requires Medicare drug plans to cover medications selected for federal price negotiation once negotiated prices take effect, and by 2026 all ten first-round drugs were covered by every plan. Plans retain the ability to require prior authorization, step therapy, and/or quantity limits as formulary management tools.

### Methods

Using national Medicare Part D formulary files, 2019-2026, we compared restrictions on nine of the ten negotiated medications with those on similar drugs in the same classes not selected for negotiation. Estimates were weighted by plan enrollment.

### Results

Weighted by enrollment, step therapy on negotiated diabetes medications fell to zero by 2025 and rose to 5.0 percent in 2026, while comparators stayed below 1 percent; negotiated anticoagulants rose to 4.8 percent. Cost sharing is set by formulary tier rather than by drug and did not change. Prior authorization was near-absent in the cardiometabolic classes and near-universal in the specialty classes, with no change associated with negotiation.

### Conclusion

Guaranteed coverage does not guarantee access. In the first year of negotiated prices, universal listing coexisted with a return of step therapy on negotiated cardiometabolic drugs that comparators did not mirror, while what beneficiaries paid at the pharmacy was unchanged.

# Factors and Disparities Influencing Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors and Glucagon-like Peptide 1 Receptor Agonists Initiation in the United States: A Scoping Review of Evidence

Systematic Review

Abstract: Introduction: Health disparities affecting minority populations and result ing in poorer outcomes for disadvantaged groups have been documented in the liter ature. Sodium/glucose-cotransporter 2 (SGLT2i) inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) markedly decrease mortality from kidney and cardiovascular events. How ever, little is known about the factors and disparities that lead to differences in SGLT2i and GLP-1RA initiation across different ethnic groups. Methods: This scoping review queried databases using key terms related to disparities in the initiation of SGLT2i and GLP-1RA among high-risk populations. Relevant data from eligible studies were extracted, organized, and analyzed thematically to identify key trends and patterns in the literature. Result: Nineteen studies were included in this review. Key risk factors influencing uptake included age, provider type, race, sex, education, comorbidities, insurance, and income, with minority patients consistently showing lower rates of initiation due to systemic barri ers and socioeconomic disparities. Patients who were younger, male, had higher education or income levels, and received care from specialists were more likely to use these thera pies. Conclusion: The adoption of SGLT2i and GLP-1RA remains suboptimal despite their proven kidney and cardiovascular benefits. Targeted efforts to reduce socioeconomic and racial inequities based on the factors identified should be encouraged.

Keywords: disparity; medication; minority; initiation

## 1. Introduction

Health disparities are known to have a vast impact on marginalized groups within the United States (US) healthcare system, resulting in poorer outcomes [1]. This is a phenomenon that is in large due to the lack of access to adequate care, lack of provider education, and structural racism that exist within the healthcare delivery system [2]. The medication treatment to limit kidney disease progression and reduce cardiovascular mortal ity has significantly progressed in the past decade. Additionally, a 2008 US Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) mandate requiring clinical trials to assess the cardiovascular

Pharmacy 2025, 13, 46 https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmacy13020046

Pharmacy 2025, 13, 46 2 of 18 safety of all new drugs has led to a wealth of high-quality data regarding their risks and benefits [3]. Clinical data demonstrated that newer diabetes medications—glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and sodium/glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is)—offer kidney and cardiovascular protective benefits [4]. However, despite strong evidence supporting their advantages, there is limited research on prescribing patterns for these medications, particularly among populations at high risk for health disparities. Nev ertheless, it is clear that uptake has been significantly lower amongst minority populations. Therefore, we aim to examine the evidence regarding the uptake of SGLT2is and GLP-1RAs. We also aimed to identify risk factors influencing the uptake of these medications and how these factors are defined in the literature for several ethnic groups in the United States. We hope to provide solutions to enhance adoption amongst the general population based on our findings.

## 2. Methods

A scoping review was carried out by querying the PubMed, Google Scholar, and MEDLINE electronic databases, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines [5]. We also enhanced the search by using an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered search engine (Consensus) to ensure the robustness of our results.

## 1. Introduction

### 2.1. Seach Strategy

A search was conducted on the aforementioned databases from inception to October 2024. The search for articles was conducted in the English language. The key terms used were as follows: (“Race” OR “ethnicity” OR “socioeconomic status”) AND (“Black” OR “Hispanic” OR “Hispanics” OR “minority” OR “minoritized population” OR “African Americans” OR “African American”) AND (“diabetes mellitus” OR “DM” OR “chronic kidney disease” OR “CKD” OR “heart failure” OR “HF”) AND (“SGLT2i” OR “GLP-1RAs” OR “empagliflozin” OR “dapagliflozin” OR “canagliflozin” OR “liraglutide” OR “semaglu tide” OR “dulaglutide”) AND (“disparities” OR “uptake” OR “prescribing pattern” OR “use” OR “prescribe” OR “adopt” OR “adoption” OR “dispense” OR “dispensing”).

### 2.3. Data Extraction and Analysis

Data extraction pertaining to the research questions was performed by JM and ver ified by DR via an independent data extraction software using Microsoft Word Version 2502 (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). Key information related to the article, including the year of publication, journal title, first author’s information, sample size, and study design, was extracted and input into an independent data extraction depository. Information related to SGLT2i and/or GLP-1RA uptake (findings, factors, solutions) was recorded. Key findings from each included article were extracted by JM and reviewed by all authors according to the aforementioned research questions. Due to the heterogeneity of the studies, no statistical analysis was performed; rather, a narrative approach was utilized to summarize the literature.

### 2.4. Methodological Quality Assessment

The included studies were individually assessed via full-text review for methodologi cal quality by the two reviewers independently (JM and DR). The quality assessment was performed by the STROBE checklist. Studies were stratified into high-, moderate-, and low-quality based on the scores [7]. The scores were not used to include or exclude the studies for review but were instead used to describe the quality of evidence.

## 3. Results

The initial search yielded 243 studies from PubMed, Google Scholar, and Scopus. Consensus yielded 248 studies. Of those, 309 duplicates were removed in Covidence. Following this, a first screening of the article sample was conducted, and 182 articles were assessed (Figure 1). During the first screening phase, 133 articles were excluded, as they did not meet the inclusion criteria. Next, a full-text review of all 46 remaining articles was performed. Of those, 27 were excluded, resulting in only 19 relevant articles that satisfied the inclusion criteria. There was an acceptable level of screening agreement among investigators (kappa = 0.51). Research Question 1: 1. What is the current evidence available on the disparities that impact SGLT2i/GLP-1RA uptake across study participants? Table 2 summarizes the characteristics of the articles included. In total, 19 studies were included in the characteristics of the analysis. Approximately two-thirds (68.3%) of the articles were published between 2021 and 2023. The majority (n = 12; 63.2%) utilized a retrospective cohort design. The 19 citations, representing a total of approximately 12,403,354 patients, were published across 13 different journals. The majority of the studies were published in the Journal of Managed Care & Specialty Pharmacy (21%) and The Journal of the American Medical Association (21%). The first SGLT2i approved was canagliflozin, in March of 2013. Furthermore, the first GLP-1RA, Byetta (exenatide), was approved in 2005. Several risk factors that impact the uptake of SGLT2is and GLP-1RAs were identified. These risk factors include age, provider type, race, sex, education, comorbidity status, insurance type, and income. Patients using SGLT2is/GLP-1RAs were significantly younger across multiple studies analyzed. Researchers concluded that younger patients may be more adherent to these medications and able to tolerate them better than older individuals. Provider type was examined across multiple studies, and many concluded that patients that receive care from a specialist (endocrinologist) are more likely to receive a prescrip tion for SGLT2is/GLP-1RAs compared to patients that receive care from a primary care physician.
